plan: [Value = $25. In a 5-bidder third-price sealed-bid auction, symmetric equilibrium is linear: bid = (4/3) × value (derivation: best-response calculus with opponents using linear bids gives coefficient 4/3). No history to update on. To maximize long-run profit against similar opponents, bid the equilibrium amount, rounded to $0.1.]

[Assume other bidders bid their true values. If I bid b and win, that means all four others ≤ b; then expected third-highest equals the second-highest among four draws = (3/5)b. Win probability = (b/49)^4. Expected profit = (b/49)^4*(18 - 0.6b). Maximize w.r.t b → b = (4/3)*18 = 24. So overbidding to $24 maximizes expected payoff under this model.]

[In a 5-player third-price auction, if opponents bid their values, I win only if all four others < my bid (probability (b/49)^4). Conditional on that, the expected payment equals the second-highest of four iid Uniform(0,b), which has mean 3/5 b. Expected payoff ≈ (b/49)^4*(31 - 0.6b). Differentiating gives optimum b ≈ 124/3 ≈ 41.33. I therefore bid near this optimum (rounded to $0.1) to maximize expected profit under plausible opponent behavior.]

[I have a low private value ($4). In a 5-bidder, third-price auction the winner pays the third-highest bid, which is likely to exceed $4 when others bid positively. To avoid winning at a loss and maximize expected profit, I will not compete—place the minimum bid (0) so I only win if the clearing price is ≤ my value, which is extremely unlikely.]

[I am Ethel with value 41 in a third-price auction. With no history, assume opponents bid their values (uniform 0–49). If I bid >49 I win for sure and pay the expected 2nd-highest of four others = 49*(3/5)=29.4, yielding expected profit 41-29.4=11.6. To secure the win with 0.1 increments, bid 49.1 to capture this positive expected surplus.]
